newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank sticks to M3 target despite volatility.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank sticks to M3 target despite volatility.

text.p: Germany's Bundesbank on Thursday vowed to stick to M3 money supply growth as one of its key policy targets, despite recent strong fluctuations which triggered criticisms about its long-term usefulness.

"Despite the increase in fluctuations in M3 money supply growth and the greater need for explanation, the Bundesbank continues to consider it an appropriate base for its policies because in the longer term, inflation continues to be a monetary problem," Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer told a news conference.

M3 money supply, which comprises cash in circulation, time, sight and short-term savings deposits, is considered to foreshadow future inflation developments and has therefore long been favoured by the inflation conscious Bundesbank.

In recent years, however, M3 has repeatedly missed the growth targets set by the Bundesbank, prompting critics to say the target was no longer relevant, particularly as inflation remained moderate despite strong M3 growth.
On the other hand Tietmeyer also said what independent economists had long expected, revealing a more pragmatic approach.

"Due to the rather large fluctuations in money supply growth developments we are focusing more strongly on the medium term trends and in the end we also continue to eye, as we have done in the past, the total monetary picture," Tietmeyer said.

Earlier this week Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said there was no automatic link between M3 growth and policy actions. For example the Bundesbank last April cut interest rates at a time of very strong M3 growth, a step that would have been impossible had the council slavishly based all its decisions only on M3 growth.

While M3 growth again got off to a very strong start this year, outpacing the year's 3.5 to 6.5 percent target corridor by growing at an 11.7 percent rate in January and 9.1 percent in February, Issing on Thursday said he expected the March data would show more moderate growth.
The numbers are expected to be released in the next few days.
Several economists have predicted the headline figure would be around 8.5 percent, and said the volume of money in circulation was likely to be a bit larger than in February.

They said that monetary capital formation likely picked up a bit in the last month, but that growth remained strong as private sector lending likely remained buoyant because the economy was showing early signs of recovery.

But economists also noted the Bundesbank was still clinging to its wish to have the future European Central Bank implement M3 growth as a key policy indicator. Other nations for example target either prices or exchange rates.
"They are going to fight for this instrument, especially now as decisions are being made about the ECB," said Irgeen Rust, a monetary economist at WestLB in Duesseldorf.
But lobbying efforts may be difficult, particularly as even the Bundesbank has repeatedly failed to meet its targets, economists said.
Looking further ahead, economists said that M3, while currently playing a clearly less important role, might again gain more prominence.

"Possibly by the fall, when M3 will probably still be fairly strong and the Bundesbank will realise that it needs to tighten rates again, they could be quite happy to trot out the M3 argument and say that it demands a rate hike," said one London-based economist.
